specPoints.text: describe the advantages and disadvantages of methods of large-scale electricity production from various renewable and non-renewable resources

primer.text: Every resource that can power a country asks for a different price: fuel, reliability, pollution or landscape. These lessons weigh the advantages and disadvantages of each large-scale generation method — the comparison exam questions are built on.

lessons.title: Fossil fuels and nuclear
lessons.opening: The two non-renewable heavyweights dominate today's supply because they are reliable and energy-dense. Their price is paid elsewhere: carbon dioxide and acid rain from fossil combustion, and radioactive waste plus accident risk from the atom.
keyPoints: Fossil fuels are reliable, respond quickly to demand changes, but are non-renewable.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming, and sulphur dioxide, which causes acid rain.
Nuclear power is reliable, emits no greenhouse gases during generation, and extracts large energy from small fuel amounts.
Nuclear stations produce radioactive waste needing safe disposal for thousands of years and carry accident risk.
Both resources are non-renewable, and nuclear stations are slow and expensive to build with no fast response to demand.

low.restatement: Two steady giants: coal, oil and gas answer the door whenever demand knocks, but their smoke warms the planet and sours the rain. The atom answers too, smoke-free and incredibly concentrated, yet leaves waste no one wants and stations that take decades.
low.analogy: A lorry and a safe-deposit vault: the lorry (fossil) delivers instantly but trails exhaust; the vault (nuclear) holds staggering value but is costly to build and its contents need guarding for millennia.
low.examPointer: For each disadvantage, name the gas or the waste explicitly — carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide for fossil; radioactive waste for nuclear — vague 'pollution' loses marks.

medium.restatement: Reliability is the shared strength: both resources generate consistently regardless of weather. The cost structures differ — fossil pays continuously in fuel and emissions (CO2 and sulphur dioxide), nuclear pays in capital, build time and a long-lived radioactive legacy, with no greenhouse output during generation but no quick throttle either.
medium.analogy: Two restaurants: the fossil diner buys ingredients every day and vents its smoke; the nuclear banquet buys almost nothing per meal but built the kitchen over a decade and buries its leftovers under a mountain.
medium.examPointer: When comparing, pair each resource with one advantage AND one disadvantage stated in cause — 'reliable because fuel supply is constant', 'warming because carbon dioxide traps radiation'.

check.stem: Which gas from burning fossil fuels contributes to global warming?

options.text: carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Fossil combustion releases CO2, a greenhouse gas.

options.text: oxygen
options.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion; it is not the emitted problem gas.

options.text: nitrogen
options.explanation: Nitrogen dominates air but is not the warming culprit here.

options.text: hydrogen
options.explanation: Hydrogen is not a fossil combustion product.

check.stem: Which disadvantage belongs to nuclear power rather than to fossil fuels?

options.text: radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years
options.explanation: The long-lived waste legacy is uniquely nuclear.

options.text: produces carbon dioxide during generation
options.explanation: Nuclear generation emits no greenhouse gases.

options.text: reliant on the weather
options.explanation: Both are reliable; neither is weather-dependent.

options.text: runs out of fuel within a year
options.explanation: Both are non-renewable but neither runs out that fast.

check.stem: A country needs a power station that responds quickly to sudden demand. Which resource fits best?

options.text: fossil fuels
options.explanation: Fossil plants can be turned up quickly to meet demand spikes.

options.text: nuclear
options.explanation: Nuclear stations cannot be switched on or off quickly.

options.text: either would do equally
options.explanation: Their response speeds differ sharply.

options.text: neither can respond to demand at all
options.explanation: Fossil generation is specifically quick-responding.

check.stem: Which statement pairs a resource with a correct advantage?

options.text: nuclear — large energy from small amounts of fuel
options.explanation: Energy density is a headline nuclear advantage.

options.text: fossil fuels — they never run out
options.explanation: Fossil fuels are non-renewable and will run out.

options.text: nuclear — it responds instantly to demand changes
options.explanation: Nuclear is slow to throttle.

options.text: fossil fuels — they produce no emissions
options.explanation: Combustion emits carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide.

check.stem: Why do nuclear power stations cost so much to establish?

options.text: they take many years to build and are expensive to build and maintain
options.explanation: Capital cost and build time are the stated disadvantages.

options.text: their fuel is the most expensive per joule
options.explanation: Nuclear's small fuel amounts are an advantage, not a cost.

options.text: they must be rebuilt every few years
options.explanation: The opposite — the build itself is the long part.

options.text: they cannot produce large amounts of energy
options.explanation: Large, consistent output is their strength.

check.stem: Name the two greenhouse-related emissions problems caused by burning fossil fuels.
check.modelAnswer: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming, and sulphur dioxide, which causes acid rain.

check.stem: State one advantage and one disadvantage of nuclear power.
check.modelAnswer: An advantage: no greenhouse gases are produced during electricity generation. A disadvantage: radioactive waste is produced that must be safely disposed of for thousands of years.

check.stem: Explain why a country cannot rely on nuclear stations alone to follow a daily demand curve.
check.modelAnswer: Nuclear stations throttle slowly, so they cannot follow sudden changes in demand. A demand curve with morning and evening peaks needs resources that respond quickly, which is why quick-responding fossil generation complements steady nuclear output.

check.stem: A town replaces its coal station with a nuclear one. State one improvement and one new concern the townspeople should expect.
check.modelAnswer: The improvement: electricity generation no longer releases carbon dioxide or sulphur dioxide. The new concern: radioactive waste is now produced locally and must be transported and disposed of safely for thousands of years.

lessons.title: Biofuels and wind
lessons.opening: Biofuels grow their fuel in fields; wind harvests the moving air. Both are renewable, but their weaknesses differ: biofuels compete with food for land, and wind only works while the weather cooperates.
keyPoints: Biofuels can count as carbon neutral because the carbon dioxide released by combustion was absorbed while the crop grew.
Biofuel crops vie with food farming for the same ground and inputs, and clearing land can release stored carbon.
Wind power is renewable with no greenhouse gases or fuel costs once the turbines are built.
Wind is unreliable: it generates only when the wind blows at sufficient speed.
Wind farms draw criticism for visual and noise pollution and carry a high initial build cost.

low.restatement: A biofuel plant is a carbon round-trip — the crop inhales what the engine exhales. A wind turbine is free-running but moody: no wind, no watts, whatever the timetable says.
low.analogy: The biofuel is a recycling bin that refills itself; the wind turbine is a fair-weather employee — brilliant on breezy days, idle in a calm.
low.examPointer: Quote 'carbon neutral' with the mechanism (absorption during growth balancing combustion) and give 'unreliable' its wind-speed condition.

medium.restatement: Biofuels balance carbon across the growth-combustion cycle, yet land economics cut against them: food competition, deforestation and point-of-use emissions. Wind converts a renewable flow with no operating emissions, but its output tracks the weather — sufficient-speed winds only — and siting debates raise visual and noise objections.
medium.analogy: Two farms: one grows fuel and competes with the kitchen; the other grows nothing but earns whenever the breeze clocks in.
medium.examPointer: State both halves of the biofuel carbon argument — absorption in growth AND release at combustion — before calling it carbon neutral.

check.stem: Why can biofuels be described as carbon neutral?

options.text: the carbon dioxide released on burning was absorbed as the crop grew
options.explanation: Growth and combustion cancel across the cycle.

options.text: they release no carbon dioxide at any point
options.explanation: Combustion still releases CO2 at the point of use.

options.text: they absorb carbon dioxide while being burned
options.explanation: Burning emits; growing absorbs.

options.text: they contain no carbon at all
options.explanation: Biofuels are carbon-based fuels.

check.stem: Which disadvantage is specific to wind power among the renewables?

options.text: it only generates when the wind blows at sufficient speed
options.explanation: Unreliability is wind's defining weakness.

options.text: its fuel is expensive to buy each year
options.explanation: Wind has no fuel costs once built.

options.text: it floods large valleys when built
options.explanation: That is the hydroelectric disadvantage.

options.text: it works only in estuaries
options.explanation: Estuaries are the tidal constraint.

check.stem: What do biofuel crops and food crops compete for?

options.text: land and resources
options.explanation: Growing fuel displaces growing food.

options.text: electricity Grid connections
options.explanation: Competition is agricultural, not electrical.

options.text: wind speeds
options.explanation: Weather is irrelevant to cropping.

options.text: radioactive waste storage
options.explanation: Nothing nuclear is involved.

check.stem: Which pair lists one advantage and one disadvantage of wind power?

options.text: renewable and no operating emissions; unreliable without sufficient wind
options.explanation: The classic wind trade-off.

options.text: cheap to build; reliable at all times
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: build cost is high, output is weather-bound.

options.text: reliable at all times; heavy fuel costs
options.explanation: Wind is neither always-on nor fuel-fed.

options.text: no noise at all; unlimited suitable sites
options.explanation: Noise pollution and siting limits are both cited.

check.stem: Clearing forest to plant biofuel crops creates which additional problem?

options.text: stored carbon is released and habitats are destroyed
options.explanation: Deforestation undoes the carbon balance and removes ecosystems.

options.text: the crops absorb too much carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Extra absorption would be a benefit, not a problem.

options.text: the fuel becomes radioactive
options.explanation: Nothing radioactive is involved.

options.text: wind speeds drop over the fields
options.explanation: Weather is unaffected by cropping.

check.stem: State the reliability weakness of wind generation.
check.modelAnswer: Wind power is unreliable: it generates only while the wind blows hard enough.

check.stem: State two running-cost advantages of wind power once the turbines are built.
check.modelAnswer: Once built, a wind farm charges nothing for fuel and little to keep it running.

check.stem: Explain why growing biofuel crops on cleared forest land can still increase atmospheric carbon dioxide overall.
check.modelAnswer: Clearing the forest releases the carbon stored in the trees and destroys the habitat, while the new crops need years to absorb comparable amounts. Combustion of the harvested fuel then releases carbon dioxide at the point of use, so the balance can stay in the atmosphere's disfavour.

check.stem: A windy region plans a wind farm near a village. State one benefit and one local objection the planners should expect.
check.modelAnswer: The benefit: renewable electricity with no greenhouse gases or pollution during operation and no fuel costs. The objection: visual pollution of the landscape and noise pollution from the turbines.

lessons.title: Hydroelectric, tidal and solar
lessons.opening: Water and light close the comparison. Dams deliver on demand but drown valleys; tides keep an impeccable schedule but fit few coastlines; solar cells serve remote places yet only work while the Sun shines.
keyPoints: Hydroelectric power is reliable, responds quickly to demand and costs nothing in fuel once built.
Hydroelectric reservoirs flood whole valleys, wiping out habitats and displacing the wildlife that lived there.
Tidal power is highly predictable because tides follow regular cycles, but few estuaries suit a barrage.
Solar cells emit nothing in operation and serve remote areas, but only generate while the Sun shines.
A single solar cell yields only a trickle of electricity, so installations need many cells and a high initial outlay.

low.restatement: The dam is the on-call worker — always ready, but its reservoir drowned a valley. The tide is the timetable-keeper — punctual to the minute, if your coastline plays along. The solar cell is the fair-weather friend with a tiny per-panel wage.
low.analogy: Three employees: one on-call (hydro), one with a fixed shift schedule (tidal), one who only shows up in sunshine and must be hired in the hundreds (solar).
low.examPointer: Match each resource to its site constraint — estuaries for tidal, sunshine for solar, valleys for hydro — and pair 'unreliable' with its weather condition.

medium.restatement: Hydroelectric trades habitat for dispatchability: reservoirs flood land, yet the station answers demand quickly with no fuel bill. Tidal gains predictability from the tide cycle but loses on site availability and aquatic impact. Solar's operating cleanliness and remote-area usefulness are undercut by sunshine dependence, small per-cell output and high initial cost.
medium.analogy: A dam is a hired hall (ready when booked, but the booking flooded the meadow); a barrage is a railway timetable (perfect schedule, few stations); solar is a big choir of quiet voices (clean, but each sings softly and only by day).
medium.examPointer: For 'reliable', attach the reason — hydro responds to demand, tides are predictable — and for solar's unreliability, name the sunshine condition explicitly.

check.stem: Which renewable resource is the most predictable in its output timing?

options.text: tidal power
options.explanation: Tides follow regular, predictable cycles.

options.text: wind power
options.explanation: Wind is the classic unreliable resource.

options.text: solar power
options.explanation: Sunshine hours vary day to day.

options.text: biofuels
options.explanation: Biofuel supply follows harvests, not a daily timetable.

check.stem: What is the main environmental cost of building a hydroelectric reservoir?

options.text: flooding large areas, destroying habitats and displacing wildlife
options.explanation: The valley pays for the dispatchability.

options.text: releasing sulphur dioxide during generation
options.explanation: Hydroelectric generation emits nothing.

options.text: producing radioactive waste
options.explanation: Nothing nuclear is involved.

options.text: noise pollution across the estuary
options.explanation: Noise belongs to wind criticisms.

check.stem: Why are there few suitable locations for tidal barrages?

options.text: they need estuaries with the right tidal conditions
options.explanation: Estuaries are the scarce siting requirement.

options.text: they need hot, dry deserts
options.explanation: That suits nothing in these notes.

options.text: they need high mountain valleys
options.explanation: Valleys are the hydroelectric terrain.

options.text: they need constant strong sunshine
options.explanation: Sunshine is the solar constraint.

check.stem: Why do solar installations need many cells?

options.text: each cell produces only a small amount of electricity
options.explanation: Scaling up means multiplying panels.

options.text: each cell lasts only a few days
options.explanation: Lifespan is not the constraint cited.

options.text: cells only work in pairs
options.explanation: No such rule exists.

options.text: each cell needs its own fuel supply
options.explanation: Sunlight is free.

check.stem: Which statement about hydroelectric and solar power together is correct?

options.text: both produce no greenhouse gases during operation, but only hydroelectric responds quickly to demand
options.explanation: Solar output follows sunshine; hydro throttles.

options.text: both are unreliable because both depend on weather
options.explanation: Hydroelectric is reliable; stored water answers on demand.

options.text: both need estuaries to function
options.explanation: Neither needs an estuary.

options.text: both produce large fuel bills
options.explanation: Neither has fuel costs.

check.stem: State the reliability advantage that hydroelectric and tidal power share.
check.modelAnswer: Both are reliable: hydroelectric responds quickly to changes in demand, and tidal output follows the very predictable tide cycle.

check.stem: State the weather condition that limits solar generation.
check.modelAnswer: Solar cells only generate electricity while the Sun is shining.

check.stem: Explain why a remote mountain hut with no mains connection is a good fit for solar cells.
check.modelAnswer: Solar cells need no Grid connection, no fuel deliveries and no turbine hall — just sunlight on panels. Where the mains never reaches, the cells' operating simplicity outweighs their sunshine dependence for small, daytime needs.

check.stem: An island community chooses tidal power over wind. State one reason supporting the choice and one cost they accept.
check.modelAnswer: Supporting reason: tides are very predictable, so generation follows a reliable schedule with no greenhouse gases or fuel costs. The cost accepted: few suitable estuary locations exist, and the barrage can harm aquatic life and disrupt shipping.

glossary.definition: Describes an energy resource that can produce energy at any time.
Describes a resource that only produces energy some of the time, such as when it is windy.
Describes a fuel whose released carbon dioxide is balanced by the carbon dioxide absorbed while its source grew.
Describes an energy resource consumed faster than it is replenished, so its supply will eventually run out.
